title: How to read Revelation
hook: apocalypse means unveiling, not catastrophe; its images reveal who really rules

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the block of great thinkers around a long, unfinished table. Your line was join the conversation. Which thinker did you pull up a chair for? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-seven.

Zombies in the streets. Cities underwater. A lone survivor with a dog and a shotgun. When a movie poster says apocalypse, that's what it's selling: the end of everything, as loud as possible. So it can come as a surprise to open the last book of the Bible, the one some people call the Apocalypse, and find that it begins with a blessing, and a greeting, and grace and peace. There are strange beasts in it, yes. Fire and trumpets and a dragon. But the book is not mainly about how the world ends. It's about what's really going on underneath the world. For the next weeks, this path reads it slowly. Today, before the first verse, a key for the lock: the word on the front door.
screen: `A BOOK THAT OPENS WITH GRACE AND PEACE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. In Greek, the book's very first word is apokalypsis. It means an uncovering, an unveiling: the cloth pulled off something that was there all along. The King James Bible translates it this way: "The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass." A revelation, not a catastrophe. Second, what gets unveiled. John writes to churches, some of them under pressure, in a world where other powers looked like they owned everything. Revelation pulls back the curtain and shows another throne, in heaven, and on it the one who actually rules. Here is the scene that holds the key. John sees a sealed scroll, and weeps because no one can open it. An elder tells him: "Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book." John turns to see the lion, and what he sees is this: "a Lamb as it had been slain." A lion is announced; a wounded lamb appears. Some readers see the whole book in that one turn: for them, power, unveiled, looks like self-giving love. Third, how Christians read it. Some read it mainly as a letter to churches in John's own day. Some read much of it as about the end of history. Some read it as a picture of every age, the same struggle again and again. Churches weigh these readings differently, and some readers combine them. Fourth, its tone. Many readers find that, read slowly, it sounds like courage, not panic. Near its end, it promises: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes." That's where the unveiling is headed.

Here's the practice: read slowly, without fear. Settle, and breathe. Hear one line from the book's opening, and just let it sit: "Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy." Notice that the book begins by blessing the one who reads it. If strange images or old fears about the end come up, let them pass like weather. If you pray, you can ask to see what's really there. If you don't, just rest with the idea that something true might be under the surface of today. The bell holds the time.
Apocalypse. From the Greek apokalypsis, an uncovering. Not the end of the world: the cloth pulled off, to show who really rules.
Your line: an unveiling. Today, when a headline sounds like the end of the world, ask one quiet question: what is this revealing, and about whom? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Christians read Revelation in different ways: some churches read it chiefly as a message to its first readers, some as prophecy of the end, and some as a picture for every age; its hymns are sung in worship across churches.

notes: ἀποκάλυψις as the first word of Revelation in Greek and its sense 'uncovering, unveiling' — standard lexicon (BDAG); the outline hook states the meaning. Confirm.
'Small churches under pressure, in a world where an empire looked like it owned everything' — a general historical framing of the book's setting (Roman Asia); no dates given. Confirm acceptable.
Three readings (preterist-leaning, futurist, idealist) named without ranking and without labels.
'A wounded lamb' paraphrases 'a Lamb as it had been slain'; confirm.
